conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having really bad abdominal pain for about a week, and last night I had over 20 watery bowel movements. It feels like my Crohn’s is flaring up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned Crohn’s—can you tell me more about your history with it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I had most of my colon removed years ago. I’ve tried several medications, but nothing’s worked long-term. I’m on steroids now and had to increase my dose a bit last week because I felt worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. Your labs show your white blood cell count is elevated, which supports an active flare. We’ve also started you on IV fluids and gave you some pain medication in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The pain is mostly in my lower left side and back, and it moves toward my stomach. Heat helps a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your exam shows tenderness in the upper quadrants, but no signs of a surgical emergency. We’re going to start you on IV steroids to help calm the inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s what usually helps. But I’m worried—could this be something else, like an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We tested your stool for C. diff, and it came back negative. We’re also checking for parasites and viruses, but so far no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’ve also noticed some blood when I wipe—should I be concerned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely from irritation due to frequent bowel movements. We didn’t see blood in your stool sample, so it’s probably not coming from deep in the intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about the chest X-ray I had? Anything show up there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a small shadow at the base of your left lung. It could be early pneumonia or just some collapsed lung tissue from shallow breathing due to pain. You don’t have a fever or cough, so we think it’s likely benign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. But if you develop a fever or cough, let us know immediately. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. What’s the plan for my pain and diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you IV methylprednisone three times a day. For pain, you’ll get Dilaudid and Tylenol as needed. We’ve also added cholestyramine to help with the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken cholestyramine before. What does it do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps bind bile acids that can worsen diarrhea in people who’ve had bowel surgery. It’s often helpful in cases like yours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, okay. And I’m still taking loperamide, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your usual loperamide. We’ll watch your bowel movements closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your symptoms are improving—your bowel movements have slowed and are more formed. That’s a good sign the treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I feel a bit better. Less cramping. What about those test results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV test came back negative, which is great—no viral infection. Stool tests for parasites and other pathogens were also negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely a Crohn’s flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all signs point to that. No infection found, and your history and symptoms match perfectly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Can I start eating again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to advance your diet to regular food today. Start slowly and let us know if you feel bloated or nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And the IV steroids—will I stay on those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll transition you to oral prednisone today. You’ll take 40 mg daily for now, then discuss tapering with your gastroenterologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was on 25 mg when I came in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were, but because this is a significant flare, we’re increasing it temporarily to get better control before starting the taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my kidney stone? I had one before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We didn’t do a new scan this time, but given your history, we recommend you follow up with urology to monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that. Any other follow-up I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you should see your primary care doctor to review steroid precautions—like bone health and infection prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. You’re eating normally, pain is controlled, and your bowels are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take prednisone 40 mg daily, omeprazole once a day, loperamide as needed, cholestyramine twice a day, and Percocet for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll follow up with GI soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, within the next week. They’ll help adjust your steroid taper and long-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep an eye on your symptoms, and call if you develop fever, worsening pain, or breathing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.
